motion: Too many kids go to college.

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: Better counseling and real exposure to work correct that imbalance. But an assumed next step is not proof that too many attend; students can reconsider, and access remains good, so the motion fails.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Welcome. Tonight's motion is that too many kids go to college; Alice supports it, and Nigel opposes it. Each debater gets thirty seconds for an opening statement, followed by two and a half minutes of crossfire. Then each receives thirty seconds for a closing statement. I will give a ten-second cue before each timed segment ends.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: College is valuable, but treating it as the default sends many young people into costly, unfocused paths. We should respect work, training, and purposeful choices equally.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Why call it too many when you would limit options-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Wait, let her answer the question.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The issue is not forbidding anyone from attending. It is the pressure that tells every teenager college is the only respectable route, even before they know their goal.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I can give you ten seconds to wrap this round.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: When expectations replace judgment, too many kids enter college for the wrong reasons. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Let's hear from Nigel.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Alice calls college pressure, but pressure to explore a future is not coercion. Young people change their minds, and college can give them room to discover interests. Training routes matter, yet they should be added, not used to steer kids away from learning. A broad education builds confidence, curiosity, and flexibility when plans change.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The answer is better guidance and stronger alternatives, not declaring students excessive simply because their path is academic. Choice, not sorting, serves kids. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: And that concludes round one. And now we move onto round two, and in round two the debaters address one another directly. This round runs two and a half minutes from the moment I finish. I will call ten seconds before the end.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: You say kids enter for the wrong reasons, but uncertainty is not a wrong reason. College is where many people test interests safely before committing to one narrow path.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If college is truly the right default, why should a teenager with no clear academic goal take years of classes instead of first trying work or training? Explain that.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Families also worry about housing, schedules, and social life, which deserve attention. But those issues do not show excess enrollment; opportunity is not overuse, so the motion fails.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: On your point about opportunity, an open door is not the same as wise pressure to walk through it. Real opportunity includes respected routes that do not require college.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Consider a student who loves repairing machines but later wants to design better ones. College builds writing and problem-solving skills, preserving options; enrollment is not excess, as the motion claims.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I agree college can broaden a student's choices. But your machine example assumes every student needs a campus first; many learn those skills through paid work, so too many are pushed toward college.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: When a student wants a field requiring advanced study, college is the right choice. That does not make students without that goal excessive; choice should fit each student, so the motion fails.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If choice should fit each student, why do schools signal that college is the successful choice before students have explored other work? Doesn't that message create the excess I describe?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: No young person should be treated as excessive for seeking education. Society benefits when people keep learning, whether they enter college with a firm plan or discover one there, so the motion fails.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your point that no individual is excessive dodges the pattern. A system can praise each applicant yet channel far too many into one route, leaving other talents underused and-

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: That is not a dodge; people are not a pile to be managed. If other routes need respect, build them up, but do not call college seekers too many.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I agree nobody should be reduced to a number. Still, calling a system crowded is not insulting students; it challenges the message that college is the only serious future, and the motion stands.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your claim that college is presented as the only serious future is the weak link. Parents and teachers can praise training without declaring education excessive, so your conclusion does not follow.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You have ten seconds left.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If you can praise training without calling education excessive, why has college become the assumed next step for-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: That's time. Let's move on to Round three, closing statements from each debater in turn. Our resolution is, whether too many kids are going to college. Leading off with her closing statement, Alice.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Nigel says uncertainty belongs in college. Yet uncertainty is exactly why no single expensive, academic route should be treated as the default. Young people deserve time to test work, craft, service, and study without being ranked by one credential. College remains right for many, but social pressure sends too many there before they can choose wisely.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: That pressure narrows classrooms and leaves other paths understaffed. We can honor college while ending the idea that it is every kid's first obligation. A fairer system opens real choices, and that-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I'll give you ten more seconds to nail this.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you. Time is up on that. And now Nigel.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Alice mistakes weak guidance for too many students learning. The remedy is to improve counseling, make training visible, and let every young person choose. Calling attendance excessive turns a personal aspiration into a social mistake. College can offer exploration, transferable skills, and a second chance for a student whose plans are still forming. We should expand choices, not shrink the path.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds warning.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Kids deserve alternatives that are genuinely respected, but they also deserve open access to college. Their uncertainty is a reason to support them, not exclude them. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you, Alice and Nigel, for a thoughtful debate; this concludes our discussion of the motion for tonight.
